title: Simple vs compound interest
examples: What is the difference between the two types of interest?
Can you show me how to calculate this using a table?
If I leave money for longer, which interest type is better?

explain.say: Today we look at two ways money grows. One is simple interest. This means interest is only earned on the original amount.
The formula for simple interest is I equals P times R times T. P is the principal, R is the rate, and T is the time.
For compound interest, the interest earns interest too. This is like a snowball rolling downhill. We use a year-by-year table to see this.
Let us compare both with one hundred pounds at five percent for three years. Simple interest adds the same amount each year. Compound interest adds more each year.

Imagine you save money in a piggy bank. Simple interest means you earn the same amount every month. Compound interest means your earnings start earning money too. This makes your savings grow much faster over time.

items: Year 3 Interest Earned (on even more money)

draw.text: Interest on interest makes money grow.

faq.q: Which type of interest is always better for me?
faq.a: Compound interest usually pays more over time. This is because you earn interest on your previous interest. You might also ask, 'Which account pays more after three years?' or 'Is compounding always better?'

faq.q: Do I have to use a table for compound interest?
faq.a: While a table helps you see it clearly, there is a formula for compound interest too. The table just shows the step-by-step growth. You might ask, 'How do I use a table?' or 'What is the formula for compounding?'
asks: How do I use a table?
What is the formula for compounding?

faq.q: What do the letters P, R, and T stand for?
faq.a: P stands for the principal, which is your starting money. R is the annual rate as a decimal. T is the time in years. You could also ask, 'What is the principal?' or 'What does R stand for?'

faq.q: If the rate is given as ten percent, what do I do?
faq.a: You must convert the percentage to a decimal. So, ten percent becomes zero point one zero. Remember to always divide the percentage by one hundred. You might ask, 'How do I change percent to decimal?' or 'What is ten percent as a decimal?'
asks: How do I change percent to decimal?
What is ten percent as a decimal?

faq.q: Can I use the simple interest formula if the time is not in years?
faq.a: The simple interest formula I equals P times R times T requires T to be in years. If the time is in months, you must divide the months by twelve. You might ask, 'What if I have months?' or 'Does T have to be years?'
asks: Does T have to be years?

facts: Simple interest is calculated only on the original principal amount.
Compound interest calculates interest on the principal plus any previously earned interest.
To use a percentage in a formula, you must convert it to a decimal by dividing by one hundred.
The time period (T) must match the period used for the rate (R).

quiz.say: A principal of five hundred pounds earns simple interest at four percent for two years. What is the total interest earned?
quiz.why: Simple interest uses the formula I equals P times R times T. Five hundred times zero point zero four times two equals four pounds.

wrong.1: This mistake happens if you multiply the rate by the time, forgetting the principal.
wrong.2: This mistake happens if you calculate the interest for one year and use that amount for both years.
wrong.3: This mistake happens if you forget to convert the percentage rate into a decimal.

quiz.say: If you invest one hundred pounds at five percent compounded annually for two years, what is the final amount?
quiz.why: The first year is one hundred plus five pounds. The second year is five percent of one hundred five, which is two pounds fifty, making the total one hundred ten pounds and twenty-five pence.

wrong.0: This mistake happens if you calculate the interest as if it were simple interest for two years.
wrong.1: This mistake happens if you only calculate the interest for the first year and stop there.
wrong.2: This mistake happens if you incorrectly calculate the percentage increase in the second year.

quiz.say: A bank offers simple interest at three percent or compound interest at three percent for four years. Which will result in more money?
quiz.why: Compound interest is always better over multiple years because you earn interest on the interest you already earned. Simple interest only uses the starting amount.

wrong.1: This mistake assumes that the interest earned each year is identical for both methods.
wrong.2: This mistake forgets that compounding allows the money to grow faster each year.
wrong.3: While the principal matters, for any positive rate and time, compounding will eventually be greater.
